content: Nuclear fuel refers to any material capable of being consumed to generate nuclear energy, analogous to how chemical fuels are burned to produce energy. The most common nuclear fuels are heavy fissile elements, such as uranium-235 (²³⁵U) and plutonium-239 (²³⁹Pu), which can sustain nuclear fission chain reactions in reactors. These fuels may exist as raw materials or as physical objects like fuel rods or bundles, often combined with structural, neutron moderating, or neutron reflecting materials. The nuclear fuel cycle encompasses the processes of mining, refining, purifying, utilizing, and disposing of these materials. This cycle is critical for nuclear power generation and nuclear weapons development. Not all nuclear fuels are used in fission chain reactions; for instance, plutonium-238 (²³⁸Pu) and other isotopes are employed in radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) to produce power through radioactive decay. Light isotopes like tritium (³H) serve as fuel for nuclear fusion. Uranium dioxide (UO₂), a common oxide fuel, has low thermal conductivity, which is influenced by porosity and burn-up. During use, fission products such as lanthanides dissolve into the lattice, while others like palladium precipitate. Fission gases like xenon and krypton form bubbles, and radiation damages the lattice. These factors can cause overheating in the pellet's center and reduce thermal conductivity. The porosity also contributes to swelling during use. Predictive equations, such as those from the International Nuclear Safety Center, relate the bulk density of UO₂ to its thermal conductivity. Advanced methods like laser flash analysis are used to measure thermal conductivity under various conditions. Mixed oxide (MOX) fuel, a blend of plutonium and uranium, behaves similarly to enriched uranium fuel and is an alternative to low-enriched uranium (LEU) in light water reactors. MOX fuel helps dispose of surplus plutonium through transmutation, though it introduces new disposal challenges. Reprocessing of spent nuclear fuel to produce MOX is conducted in countries like France, England, Russia, India, and Japan. The United States, however, has not permitted commercial fuel reprocessing due to nonproliferation concerns. Metal fuels, such as uranium-zirconium alloys, offer higher thermal conductivity than oxide fuels but cannot withstand equally high temperatures. TRIGA (Training, Research, Isotopes, General Atomics) reactors use uranium-zirconium-hydride (UZrH) fuel, which has a prompt negative temperature coefficient, making meltdowns physically impossible. These reactors are often used for research purposes, with many located in the USA and other countries. Actinide fuels, used in fast neutron reactors, include minor actinides produced by neutron capture in uranium and plutonium. Metal actinide fuels, typically alloys of zirconium, uranium, plutonium, and minor actinides, are inherently safe due to thermal expansion increasing neutron leakage. Ceramic fuels, such as uranium nitride (UN) and uranium carbide (UC), have high thermal conductivities and melting points but are less understood and prone to swelling. Uranium nitride, for example, requires isotopically enriched nitrogen (¹⁵N) to avoid producing radioactive carbon-14. Uranium carbide, with its absence of oxygen, is an attractive candidate for certain Generation IV reactors like gas-cooled fast reactors. Liquid fuels, where the fuel is dissolved in the coolant, were used in experiments like the molten salt reactor experiment. These fuels can operate at high temperatures due to the high boiling points of molten salts. Aqueous homogeneous reactors, using uranium salts dissolved in water, have not been used for large power reactors due to the ease of fuel dispersion in accidents. Common physical forms of nuclear fuel include uranium dioxide pellets, which are sintered into hard ceramic forms and inserted into corrosion-resistant metal tubes (fuel rods). These rods are assembled into bundles for use in reactor cores. Pressurized water reactor (PWR) fuel consists of uranium oxide pellets in Zircaloy tubes, with helium gas filling the cladding gap to improve heat conduction. Boiling water reactor (BWR) fuel is similar but includes a thin tube surrounding each bundle to prevent local density variations. CANDU reactors use sintered uranium dioxide pellets in Zirconium alloy tubes, with bundles designed for efficient heavy water moderation. Less common fuel forms include TRISO (tristructural-isotropic) fuel particles, which consist of a uranium-based core coated with multiple layers of carbon and silicon carbide for structural integrity and fission product retention. TRISO fuels are used in high-temperature reactors like pebble bed reactors and prismatic-block gas-cooled reactors. Other forms include CerMet fuels (ceramic particles in a metal matrix) and plate-type fuels, which are used in specific research reactors. Spent nuclear fuel is a complex mixture of fission products, uranium, plutonium, and transuranic elements. It often contains nanoparticles of platinum group metals and may exhibit cracking, swelling, and near-melting-point usage. Despite these changes, spent fuel retains most actinides and fission products within the uranium dioxide lattice, making it highly insoluble in water. Post-irradiation examination (PIE) is conducted to study fuel behavior under reactor conditions. This involves both nondestructive and destructive methods in hot cells to ensure fuel safety and effectiveness. PIE is also used to investigate reactor cores after major accidents. Radioisotope decay fuels, such as those used in RTGs, generate electricity from radioactive decay. Plutonium-238 is the most widely used fuel for RTGs due to its long half-life and low radiation levels. Radioisotope heater units (RHUs) provide localized heating for sensitive equipment in deep space missions. Fusion fuels include isotopes like tritium (³H), deuterium (²H), and helium-3 (³He). First-generation fusion fuels, such as deuterium and tritium, are relatively easy to fuse. Second-generation fuels, like deuterium and helium-3, require higher confinement temperatures or longer confinement times. Third-generation fuels, producing only charged particles, represent the ultimate goal of fusion research due to minimal radioactive activation of reactor components.
